rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5 report own service implementation, LAI field validation campaigns (Figs 9, 12, 15), comparisons of suggested vs metered irrigation volumes (Figs 10, 11, 14) and farmer feedback. Q2: Section 5.1 states adoption of IRRISAT produced an increase of irrigation efficiency because water volumes were reduced relative to traditional practice; farmers on average applied 15% more than IRRISAT volumes (Figs 10-11); Abstract says most cases showed efficiency gains from reduced volumes; Section 5.2 Fig 13-14 shows standard FAO Kc would over-irrigate vs satellite-based per-parcel needs. Q4: the study measures the intermediate pathway: LAI maps validated against Licor LAI-2000 ground data (Figs 9, 12, 15), ETcrop validated with eddy covariance (Fig 2), and quantifies the gap between applied volumes and satellite CWR at farm and district level (Figs 10, 11, 14). Q5: Section 5 reports results separately for Campania Italy (maize/alfalfa, Mediterranean), Marchfeld Austria (sugarbeet, semi-arid) and Bookpurnong South Australia (citrus/vines), each with satellite-vs-applied volume comparisons. Q6: Fig 11 compares metered and suggested volumes for the 1200 ha Boscariello district; Table 2 service covers 669 farmers and 5500 ha over four irrigation consortia; Section 5.2 scheme-level CWR estimate for Marchfeld. Q7: Section 5.1 states from own observation that small farms (below ten-twelve hectares) had lower efficiency and were reluctant to adopt, attributing this to lack of metering/water pricing controls and dated equipment, whereas farms above that size adopted and tested volume reductions; Section 6 states savings are achieved by convincing farmers to limit applications within ETcrop; over-irrigation partly due to lag between advice and application. Q8: Section 5.1 notes comparison of suggested vs actual volumes is often difficult due to scarce field data and LAI underestimation above 3.5; Section 5.2 states lacking crop management and soil information so only speculation is possible; Section 5.3 states the comparison excludes precipitation and further validation is needed for a complete accuracy assessment.
rows.notes: Water-saving outcome is asserted ('it was proven') largely without directly tabulated before/after data; the Italian volume reductions over past years are attributed to water managers' estimates and metering rather than a controlled comparison. Q3 no: the saving rests on a single comparison of suggested vs metered volumes; farmer feedback concerns usefulness, not water use. Q9 no: no dispersion is given for the water-saving or volume-comparison result; <U+00B1>st.dev. in Fig 16 refers to citrus Kc, RMSE for LAI does not count.

rows.evidence: Q1: own LAI field campaigns (Figs 9, 12, 15), ETcrop validation against eddy covariance (Fig 2), and comparisons of satellite-based CWR with metered irrigation (Figs 10, 11, 14; Section 5.3 farm figures). Q2: Section 5.1 states adoption of the satellite-based service increased irrigation efficiency through reduced water volumes and that farmers applied on average 15% more than satellite-estimated requirements; Section 5.2 Figs 13-14 show satellite-based Kc for sugarbeet lower than standard FAO Kc so standard Kc would over-irrigate; Section 5.3 reports satellite-based volumes 2.8 vs 3.1 measured Ml/ha citrus and 2.8 vs 2.7 for vineyards. Q4: intermediate variables measured: LAI from satellite checked against Licor ground data (R2 0.85, RMSE 0.42 in Austria; Figs 9, 15), ETcrop checked against eddy-covariance fluxes (Fig 2), and the over-application gap quantified at farm and district scale (Figs 10, 11). Q5: results reported separately for Campania (maize, alfalfa), Marchfeld (sugarbeet) and Bookpurnong (citrus, vines) across three climates. Q6: Fig 11 district-level (1200 ha) comparison; Table 2 5500 ha across four consortia; Section 5.2 scheme-level CWR for Marchfeld; Section 5.3 farm-scale cumulative volumes. Q7: Section 5.1 states from own findings that farm size above ten-twelve hectares and metering/water pricing controls condition adoption and volume reduction; Section 6 states savings require convincing farmers to keep applications within ETcrop. Q8: Section 5.1 scarce field data for volume comparisons and LAI saturation above 3.5; Section 5.2 missing crop management and soil information; Section 5.3 comparison excludes precipitation, further validation needed.
rows.notes: The passage's statement that RS-assisted Kc converges toward standard values is not what this study shows: it reports satellite Kc below standard FAO Kc for sugarbeet and consistent-on-average but highly variable Kc for citrus; the water-saving/over-irrigation part of the claim is supported. Q3 no: water saving rests on one method (suggested vs metered volumes); LAI and ET validations verify the estimate, not the saving. Q9 no: Fig 16 gives <U+00B1>st.dev. only for citrus Kc; no dispersion for the water-saving result; LAI RMSE does not count.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is largely a description of an operational service; the water-saving results are reported briefly and partly qualitatively (Section 5.1), so Q2 'yes' for both rows carries some doubt.
